log.reply:
# Practitioner Academy Proposal for Tamarack Instruments (fictional)

**Prepared for:** Dana Whitfield, General Counsel
**Program:** Practitioner Academy, AI Governance Academy
**Format:** 2 days, live virtual, four 90-minute working sessions per day
**Price:** US$12,500
**Source:** Discovery call notes of 6 October 2026, with Dana Whitfield, Ravi Okafor and Ingrid Solberg

## 1. Situation Summary

Tamarack Instruments designs and manufactures laboratory measurement instruments. It is headquartered in the Netherlands and operates in the Netherlands, Germany and the United States, with about 1,100 staff. The Client describes its AI maturity as Piloting and its AI use as follows:

- **Deployed:** a customer service chatbot on the support portal.
- **Piloting:** AI visual inspection on the German production line.
- **Planned:** AI sales forecasting next year.

The Client's stated regulatory drivers are the EU AI Act and GDPR. ISO/IEC 42001 work is planned to start next year, and that start date is not fixed. In June 2026 an internal audit finding recorded that there is no inventory of AI systems.

The Client lists an ISO/IEC 27001 ISMS, an ISO 9001 quality management system and an internal audit function as incumbent frameworks. The extent to which records or controls under those frameworks can be reused for AI governance is Unknown, and the program will not assume any.

## 2. Why Hands-On Practitioner Capability Fits Now

The sponsor's stated objective is direct: "I want governance in place before visual inspection goes into production in Q2 2027." Meeting that objective depends on people inside the Client who can build and maintain governance artifacts themselves, not on a document delivered from outside.

The Practitioner Academy addresses this in three ways:

- **It responds to the audit finding.** Participants start the AI system inventory during the program, which responds directly to the June 2026 finding. This proposal makes no claim about how that finding will be assessed or closed.
- **It works on the Client's own systems.** Participants build in the GRC Workbook (https://github.com/rolldabones/grc-workbook) and the Slow AI Kitchen (https://github.com/rolldabones/slow-ai-kitchen) using the Client's own use cases.
- **It brings the right roles into one room.** The audience roles stated for this program are the General Counsel, CISO, Head of Quality, Head of Data, German plant manager and two internal auditors. This mix allows legal, security, quality, data, operations and assurance perspectives to work on the same artifacts at the same time.

The program is anchored in three principles: Slow AI, Informed Intent, Final Liability rests with the Human.

## 3. Running Worked Examples

Two use cases run through both days.

1. **AI visual inspection, German production line.** This is the system named in the sponsor's objective. It also carries a stated constraint: the German works council is consulted before anything touches production staff.
2. **Customer service chatbot.** This is the only deployed system. It is the natural test case for GDPR and for the stated constraint that customer data must stay in the EU.

**Sales forecasting** enters the inventory and classification exercise as a planned system, so that the inventory covers all three systems.

**Confidentiality approach.** All exercise material uses sanitized analogs:

- Chatbot exercises use synthetic support transcripts, so no real customer data leaves the EU or enters the program.
- Visual inspection exercises use synthetic defect descriptions and contain no images, records or data relating to production staff.

The exercises design governance for production staff matters but do not touch production staff. Works council consultation is built into each relevant artifact as a required gate. Whether that consultation has taken place is Unknown.

## 4. Two-Day Curriculum

The Turtle and the Phoenix is told in Session 1, using the facilitation kit at https://github.com/rolldabones/AI-Governance-Academy/blob/main/the-turtle-and-the-phoenix.md. This seats the doctrine before the instruments arrive on Day 2. The kit's handle map bridges the story to the GRC Workbook modules, and the kit's twenty-minute closing exercise runs at the close of Session 1.

**Day 1: GRC Workbook (https://github.com/rolldabones/grc-workbook)**

| Session | Exercise | Repository asset | Artifact produced |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Fable told from the kit. The handle map links story elements to the workbook modules. | Facilitation kit: the story and the handle map | Shared vocabulary linking the fable to the modules |
| 1 | Draft governance roles and decision rights for both worked examples. Owners not yet agreed are marked Unknown. | GRC Workbook: governance structures | Draft AI governance structure and decision-rights chart |
| 1 | Twenty-minute closing exercise | Facilitation kit, section 8 | The three artifacts specified in section 8 of the kit |
| 2 | Enter all three systems in the inventory and classify each provisionally against EU AI Act categories and GDPR relevance. | GRC Workbook: AI system inventories and classification | Started AI system inventory with three entries and provisional classifications |
| 3 | Assess risks and impacts for visual inspection and the chatbot. Works council consultation is recorded as a dependency for visual inspection. | GRC Workbook: risk and impact assessments | Draft risk register entries for both systems and an impact assessment outline for visual inspection |
| 4 | Draft an AI use policy skeleton and an intake procedure for adding systems to the inventory. | GRC Workbook: policies and operating procedures | Policy skeleton and draft inventory intake procedure |

**Day 2: Slow AI Kitchen (https://github.com/rolldabones/slow-ai-kitchen) plus assurance**

| Session | Exercise | Repository asset | Artifact produced |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | Write governed prompt specifications for chatbot responses using synthetic transcripts. EU data residency is declared as a constraint. | Slow AI Kitchen: governed prompting | Governed prompt specification for the chatbot |
| 6 | Design two workflows: visual inspection defect disposition and chatbot escalation to a human. | Slow AI Kitchen: practical AI workflow design | Two governed workflow drafts |
| 7 | Place human decision points and accountability in both workflows. The works council gate is included for visual inspection. | Slow AI Kitchen: human oversight and accountability | Oversight and accountability matrix, with named individuals Unknown until assigned by the Client |
| 8 | Define the evidence required for each workflow and the acceptance criteria for treating each as done. | Slow AI Kitchen: evidence collection and audit readiness, with The Definition of Done (https://github.com/rolldabones/definition-of-done) | Evidence plan and done criteria for each workflow |

The board-layer reference, AI Governance for Boards (https://github.com/rolldabones/ai-governance-for-boards), is introduced in Session 8. Its purpose is to show participants where practitioner artifacts would later be reported upward. Specific file paths within each repository are confirmed in the pre-work packet.

## 5. Deliverables

Participants leave with working drafts in the repositories, not finished instruments:

- A started AI system inventory covering the chatbot, visual inspection and sales forecasting.
- Draft risk register entries for visual inspection and the chatbot.
- At least two governed workflows: visual inspection defect disposition and chatbot escalation.
- Supporting drafts: the governance structure, the three section 8 artifacts, the policy skeleton, the intake procedure, the prompt specification, the oversight matrix and the evidence plans.

These drafts can inform later ISO/IEC 42001 preparation. The program does not promise any certification or audit outcome.

## 6. Logistics and Price

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Format | Live virtual, 2 days, four 90-minute working sessions per day |
| Price | US$12,500 |
| Dates | Unknown |
| Time zone | Unknown |
| Participant count | Seven, based on the stated audience roles |
| Budget fit | The Profile Block states a budget approved up to US$80,000 this fiscal year |

## 7. Next Step

A decision is expected by 15 December 2026. On confirmation, we will agree program dates and issue the pre-work packet. That packet will ask each participant to bring a list of AI systems in their area, any existing policies and one live workflow they want governed. Participants should prepare sanitized versions where the stated constraints require it.

Human-made, for Easy Work, Simply Done.

judgment_calls: Slow AI Kitchen 'pattern' is rendered as the Day 2 topic names (for example 'governed prompting'). The prompt's own curriculum spine names these as the Day 2 topics, so I treated them as satisfying item 4. A stricter scorer could want finer-grained pattern names.

The chatbot is called 'the natural test case for GDPR' and treated as handling customer data. Customer data is stated as a constraint, and GDPR is a stated driver. Under the v1.14.3 guidance this is a consequence of a stated constraint applied to a stated system, not a new Client fact. Another scorer could read it as an inferred state.

'Participant count: Seven, based on the stated audience roles' counts the listed roles, including 'two internal auditors', as seven attendees. I treated this as derived from AUDIENCE_ROLES rather than an invented relation.

'Responds directly to the June 2026 finding', the works council 'required gate' and the incumbent frameworks 'can be reused' (with extent Unknown) are proposed work or conditional statements. They assert no current Client state, so I did not count them as invented facts.
Session 1 holds the fable, a governance exercise and the 20-minute closing exercise inside 90 minutes. Feasibility and the two-page length are not checklist items, so I did not score them.
